meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Parks, from Rosa Parks: My Story (1992), p. 116. The popular wording is condensed: the book adds that she was not old, and that she was forty-two.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Rosa Parks: My Story, the 1992 autobiography she wrote with Jim Haskins, at page 116. Two independent sources cite that exact page for this passage — Wikiquote’s sourced Rosa Parks section ↗ and Wikipedia ↗, which footnotes it to Parks & Haskins 1992, p. 116. The attribution is not in doubt. What has happened to the wording is: between the two halves of the version in circulation, the book carries a sentence most reposts leave out — “I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two.”

source.excerpt: People always say that I didn’t give up my seat because I was tired, but that isn’t true. I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day. I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in.
trail: We read the raw wikitext of Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks page ↗ rather than a rendered summary, and its sourced section gives the full passage with the citation “Rosa Parks: My Story, p. 116, Rosa Parks and James Haskins (1992)”.

We also fetched the wikitext of Wikipedia’s Rosa Parks article ↗, which quotes the same passage and footnotes it to the identical source and page (Parks & Haskins 1992, p. 116) — an independent witness to the citation.

The book itself is held at the Internet Archive ↗, but only as a lending copy whose text we could not open. The page number therefore rests on two independent citations rather than on our own reading of p. 116 — and those two transcriptions differ on a single word, “say” against “said”, which is why this page does not treat that difference as a documented drift.

Parks made the same argument in her own handwriting years earlier: a draft in the Rosa Parks Papers ↗ puts it as “I had been pushed around all my life and felt at this moment that I couldn’t take it anymore.”
source.excerptNote: Set that against the version in circulation and the cut is obvious: the two sentences about her age disappear — which is a shame, because they are half the point she was making. One caveat on the transcription itself: Wikipedia renders the opening “People always say” and Wikiquote renders it “People always said”, both citing the same page. We have not read p. 116 ourselves, so we do not adjudicate between them.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks (1913–2005) was an American civil rights activist who served for more than a decade as secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP before her arrest on 1 December 1955 set off the Montgomery bus boycott. She published two memoirs, Rosa Parks: My Story (1992) and Quiet Strength (1994), and spent much of her later life correcting the sanded-down version of her own story.

misattribution.heading: Right author, trimmed wording
misattribution.intro: Nothing about the attribution is wrong. What has happened to this passage is quieter: it has been trimmed in transit, and the trim removes the sentence that answers the myth most directly.

items.who: The missing sentences about her age
items.why: Between “…end of a working day” and “No, the only tired I was”, the sourced text carries “I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two.” — in Wikiquote’s transcription ↗ and in Wikipedia’s ↗ alike. She was rebutting two myths at once; the popular cut keeps only one.

items.who: “She was just tired after a long day’s work”
items.tag: The myth this passage exists to refute
items.why: The tired-seamstress version is the reason Parks wrote the paragraph. She was a long-serving NAACP branch secretary, and she spent decades correcting the idea that 1 December 1955 was fatigue rather than refusal.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Rosa Parks, from Rosa Parks: My Story (1992) at p. 116 — quoted almost everywhere in a shortened form that drops her age, per Wikiquote ↗ and Wikipedia ↗, which cite the same page.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the rare case of someone outliving their own legend long enough to argue with it in print. By 1992 the tired-seamstress story was fixed in schoolbooks, and Parks used her autobiography to take it apart sentence by sentence.
The correction matters because the two versions describe different events. Fatigue is something that happens to you. Being tired of giving in is a decision.
detailsBody: Parks had been secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch since 1943, investigating and documenting cases of racial violence, and had attended the Highlander Folk School in the summer of 1955. She knew what an arrest would set in motion.
She was not the first to refuse: Claudette Colvin, fifteen, had been arrested in Montgomery that March for the same thing. What followed Parks’s arrest was a 381-day boycott of the city’s buses.
context.pull: Fatigue is something that happens to you. Being tired of giving in is a decision.
